questions.prompt: Which page-replacement algorithm can exhibit Belady's anomaly, where adding more page frames increases the number of page faults?
questions.explanation: FIFO ignores access recency, so a larger frame count can evict a page that is about to be reused. Stack algorithms such as LRU and OPT are provably immune to the anomaly.

questions.prompt: A deadlock requires four conditions to hold simultaneously. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Priority inversion is a separate scheduling problem where a high-priority task waits on a lower-priority one.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a process and a thread?

options.text: Threads have separate address spaces; processes share one
Processes have separate address spaces; threads share one

questions.explanation: Each process owns an isolated address space. Threads within a process share that space — which is why thread communication is cheap and why data races are possible.

questions.prompt: Which scheduling algorithm gives the provably minimum average waiting time for a fixed set of jobs?
questions.explanation: SJF is optimal for average waiting time, but it requires knowing burst times in advance and can starve long jobs — which is why real schedulers approximate it instead.

questions.prompt: What does thrashing refer to in an operating system?

options.text: The CPU cache being flushed on every context switch
A process consuming its entire time slice
Excessive paging activity that leaves little time for useful work
Two threads deadlocking on the same mutex

questions.explanation: Thrashing happens when the working set exceeds available physical memory, so the system spends nearly all its time swapping pages rather than executing instructions.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid solution to the critical section problem that guarantees mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting?
questions.explanation: Peterson's algorithm satisfies all three requirements for two processes. Disabling interrupts does not scale to multiprocessors, and an unsynchronised flag fails mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)?

options.text: To buffer disk writes before they are flushed
To store the contents of recently accessed pages
To hold the process control blocks of ready processes
To cache recently used virtual-to-physical address translations

questions.explanation: The TLB is a small associative cache of page-table entries. A hit avoids walking the page table, which would otherwise cost extra memory accesses on every reference.

questions.prompt: In a system using semaphores, what does a binary semaphore initialised to 1 behave as?
questions.explanation: A binary semaphore starting at 1 admits exactly one holder at a time, giving mutual exclusion. The practical difference from a true mutex is ownership: a mutex may only be released by the thread that acquired it.

questions.prompt: Which condition must hold for a system state to be considered 'safe' under the Banker's algorithm?

options.text: Every process has declared zero maximum need
There exists a sequence in which every process can finish

questions.explanation: A safe state is one where at least one ordering exists that lets every process obtain its maximum need and terminate. Unsafe does not mean deadlocked — it means deadlock can no longer be ruled out.

questions.prompt: What happens during a context switch?

options.text: The CPU saves the current process state and restores another's
The process is permanently removed from the ready queue
All cached pages are written back to disk
The scheduler recalculates every process priority

questions.explanation: The kernel saves registers, program counter and other state into the outgoing process's PCB, then loads the incoming one's. It is pure overhead, which is why excessive switching hurts throughput.
